title: The headless giant
hook: a headless giant grabs the brothers, and someone inside it is glad to see Rama
carry: the self is not the body

segments.voice: Yesterday: Jatayu's last breath, and a prince who gave a bird a son's funeral. The last rites honor love, not only blood.

The brothers head on through deep forest, and the forest gets stranger. Then the path is blocked by something Valmiki describes like a nightmare. It's as big as a hill. It has no head and no neck. Its mouth is in its belly, huge, with teeth. A single eye sits in its chest. And its two arms are so long they sweep the forest around it for anything to eat. Before the brothers can turn, those arms close around them both.
screen: `DEEPER INTO THE FOREST.` → `NO HEAD, A MOUTH IN ITS BELLY.` → `THE ARMS CLOSE.`

segments.voice: Its name is Kabandha, and as an ordinary Sanskrit word, kabandha means a headless trunk. The creature squeezes them and says plainly: you'll do for my dinner. Lakshmana is frightened, and Valmiki lets him be. Leave me as its food, he tells Rama; save yourself, and go find Sita. Rama won't hear of it. The brothers see it at the same moment: the creature's whole strength is in those arms. Rama cuts off the right arm and Lakshmana the left, and the giant crashes down. Then the strange part. Lying there armless, the creature asks who they are, and when he hears it's Rama, his whole tone changes. He's glad. He's been waiting for this, he says. He wasn't always this shape. Under the scene sits one of Hinduism's biggest teachings: the body is not the self. Inside every body, Hindus teach, is the atman, the real self, which isn't born and doesn't die. In the Bhagavad Gita, Krishna gives it a picture: as a person throws off worn-out clothes and puts on new ones, the self leaves worn-out bodies and takes on new ones. So the horror on the path is a body, a covering. Someone is inside it, and that someone knows Rama's name. It's why, when someone dies, Hindus pray: may his atma find peace. The body is gone; the self has gone on.
screen: `KABANDHA: A HEADLESS TRUNK.` · `TWO ARMS CUT; THE MONSTER IS GLAD.` · `ATMAN: THE SELF IS NOT THE BODY.` · `LIKE WORN-OUT CLOTHES.`

segments.voice: Sit still and feel your body: the weight on the chair, your hands, your breath. Then notice the one who is noticing. Many Hindu teachers give this as a simple meditation: the body is felt, and you are the one feeling it. Breathe in: this is my body. Breathe out: and I am more than it. If you pray, rest in that for a few breaths; if not, simply watch.
Kabandha. A headless trunk, all arms and belly, with someone inside waiting for Rama.
Your line: the self is not the body. Tomorrow, the monster tells his story. Day five hundred seventy-six, done.

howItsDone: Artists usually draw Kabandha as Valmiki describes him: headless, with a mouth in his belly. Hindu teachers often explain cremation through the teaching that the atman has left the body, and verses of the Bhagavad Gita are often read at funerals and prayer meetings.
